deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is not original research. It is Riemann's reading excerpt (continued from fol. 48v) of H. Brunner's German summary, in Dingler's Polytechnisches Journal vol. 125, of M. H. Jacobi's 'Théorie des machines électromagnétiques' (Bulletin phys.-math. Acad. St. Pétersbourg IX, 1850/51). Jacobi takes the geometry of the motor as given. He then asks how the useful work (Nutzeffekt) depends on four free quantities: battery EMF, number of cells, wire windings and circuit resistance.

Notation:
- k is the EMF of one cell and n the number of cells (in series).
- ϱ is the total circuit resistance.
- β is the number of windings, assumed equal in the moving and fixed electromagnets.
- Unprimed quantities refer to the machine at rest; primed ones to steady speed v.
- i is the current.
- q is the zinc dissolved per unit time.
- m is the magnetism of each electromagnet.
- μ is the mutual attraction.

Static relations, with all proportionality constants set to 1:
- (1) i = nk/ϱ (Ohm's law).
- (2) q = n·i = n²k/ϱ. Each of the n cells dissolves zinc in proportion to i (Faraday's electrochemical law, bracketed by Riemann under 'Ohm').
- (3) m = βi = βnk/ϱ (Lenz–Jacobi: magnetism ∝ ampere-turns, unsaturated iron).
- (4) μ = m² = β²n²k²/ϱ² (attraction ∝ product of the two equal magnetisms).

Back-EMF (Gegenstrom), equations (5) and (7). Motion induces a counter-current i₁ = i − i'. It is proportional to m', β and v and inversely proportional to ϱ: i₁ = α m' β v/ϱ = αβ² i' v/ϱ. Here α depends only on the 'coercive force' (really the inductive/geometric constant of the electromagnets) and slightly on the coil resistance.

Solving for the running current (implicit step, mine):
- nk/ϱ − i' = αβ² i' v/ϱ.
- Hence i' = nk/(ϱ + αβ² v).
- So (11) m' = β i' = βnk/(ϱ + αβ² v).

Steady running, equation (13): the mean mechanical resistance balances the driving attraction, R = μ' = m'².

Useful work per unit time, equation (18): T = R v.
- From √R = m', solve v = (βnk − ϱ√R)/(αβ²√R) (mine).
- Hence T = (βnk√R − Rϱ)/(αβ²).
- Equivalently T = v(βnk)²/(ϱ + αβ² v)².

Maximization, equations (20) and (22):
- Set x = √R, so T = (βnk x − ϱx²)/(αβ²).
- Then dT/dx = 0 gives x = βnk/(2ϱ).
- So R₀ = β²n²k²/(4ϱ²), i.e. R₀ = μ/4 and m'₀ = m/2.
- The maximum is T₀ = n²k²/(4ϱα).
- The corresponding speed is v₀ = ϱ/(αβ²).
- So changing β changes R₀ and v₀ but not T₀.

Economic effect ('duty'), equation (26):
- At the maximum i'₀ = i/2 = nk/(2ϱ), so zinc consumption is q'₀ = n i'₀ = n²k/(2ϱ).
- Duty E = T₀/q'₀ = k/(2α), independent of n, ϱ and β.

Purpose: to reproduce Jacobi's laws for electric motors. Maximum power occurs when the running current is half the stalled current. The maximum power is n²k²/(4αϱ). Efficiency at that point is 50%, and the duty depends only on k and α.
errors: No mathematical errors. Equations (11), (18), (20), (22) and (26) all follow correctly from (1)–(7) and (13).

Physical/attribution remark: (2), q = n·i, is Faraday's electrochemical law rather than Ohm's. The brace labelled 'Ohm' covers both (1) and (2), which is loose grouping in the excerpt, not a computational slip.
Proportionality constants are silently set to 1, e.g. μ = m², R = m'², and induced EMF ∝ m'βv. This follows Jacobi's simplified exposition; dimensionally these are proportionalities, not equalities.
Calling α a 'measure of the coercive force' is Jacobi's own (dated) interpretation. α is essentially an induction/geometry constant of the electromagnets.

results.what: Running current of a motor with back-EMF: i' = nk/(ϱ + αβ²v), hence m' = βnk/(ϱ+αβ²v)
results.modern_name: DC motor equation with back-EMF proportional to speed (I = (V − K ω)/R)
results.usually_credited_to: Lenz and Jacobi (1830s–1840s); M. H. Jacobi, 1850 memoir

results.what: Power T = Rv = (βnk√R − Rϱ)/(αβ²) maximized at R₀ = μ/4 (current halved), T₀ = n²k²/(4ϱα)
results.modern_name: Jacobi's law / maximum power transfer theorem (max power at half stall current, 50% efficiency)

results.what: Duty E = T₀/q'₀ = k/(2α), independent of number of cells, resistance and windings
results.modern_name: Efficiency (work per unit zinc consumed) of a battery-driven motor at maximum power

deep.surprise_reason: This is explicitly a reading excerpt of Brunner's summary of Jacobi's 1850 memoir in Dingler's Polytechnisches Journal 125. All results are Jacobi's well-known motor laws, reproduced faithfully with no original contribution by Riemann. It is only of mild interest as evidence of Riemann's reading in applied electromagnetism.

checkable.sympy: n,k,rho,al,be,v=symbols('n k rho alpha beta v',positive=True); ip=symbols('ip'); simplify(solve(Eq(n*k/rho-ip, al*be**2*ip*v/rho), ip)[0] - n*k/(rho+al*be**2*v))==0
checkable.asserts: Equation (11): the running current is i' = nk/(ϱ+αβ²v)
The two forms of the useful work in (18) agree
The maximum of T occurs at R₀ = β²n²k²/(4ϱ²) (expression simplifies to 0)
Equation (22): T₀ = n²k²/(4ϱα), independent of β
The optimal speed is v₀ = ϱ/(αβ²), which depends on β (so β changes v₀ but not T₀)

transcription_corrections: Marginal labels (5), (13) and (20) are left-margin equation numbers attached to the continuation lines; the transcription correctly places them inline.
In (18) the manuscript writes the numerator as 'βnk√R − Rϱ', consistent with the transcription.

The first, struck-out word before 'der Coercitivkraft' is illegible; it is rendered as a deletion, which is fine. 'bei angehaltener Maschine' is plausible, consistent with the unprimed (static) quantities.
